A question about moving old vault:v1: values to the newest key after rotation is testing rewrap, which needs only update on transit/rewrap/<key> and never exposes plaintext.
A question about blocking leaked old ciphertext versus permanently deleting versions is testing that raising min_decryption_version is reversible while trim after raising the minimums deletes.

quiz.q: An operator rotates the transit key `invoices` twice, so it has versions 1 to 3. A stored value begins with `vault:v1:`. Which statement about decrypting it right now is accurate?
choices: It fails, because rotation automatically makes older key versions unavailable for decryption until they are rewrapped by the application
It succeeds only if the caller adds `key_version=1` to the request, since decrypt otherwise always selects the newest version in the ring
It succeeds, because decrypt reads the version from the prefix and `min_decryption_version` has not been raised above 1
It succeeds, and Vault replaces the stored value with a `vault:v3:` ciphertext as a side effect of the decrypt operation
quiz.explain: Rotation only adds a version. Decrypt follows the ciphertext prefix, so v1 data still decrypts unless min_decryption_version is raised. Vault does not store the application's ciphertext, so it cannot replace anything; rewrap is the explicit upgrade.

quiz.q: A compliance team must keep searching an encrypted `tenant_code` column with an equality query, while different tenants must not be able to open each other's data. Which transit key setup supports both?
choices: An `ed25519` key with `derived=true`, because signature keys produce the same output for the same input and context
An `aes256-gcm96` key with `derived=true` and `convergent_encryption=true`, plus a base64 context per tenant on every call
An `aes256-gcm96` key left at its defaults, because the random nonce ensures equal plaintexts give equal ciphertext for lookup
An `rsa-4096` key with `min_encryption_version` pinned to 1, because pinning a version makes the ciphertext deterministic
quiz.explain: Convergent encryption needs a symmetric key with derivation, so equal plaintext and context give equal ciphertext. The per-tenant context separates tenants. The default uses a random nonce, and ed25519 cannot encrypt.

days.recap: Transit takes and returns base64; ciphertext vault:vN: names the key version, the caller picks the key by path. Rotate adds a version; rewrap upgrades ciphertext without exposing plaintext. min_decryption_version blocks reversibly, trim deletes. Convergent encryption needs derived=true and a context.

days.title: Vault Encryption: Barrier, Keyring, Initialization, Seal and Unseal, and Environment Variables

concepts.heading: The Security Barrier and Untrusted Storage
concepts.body: Vault treats its storage backend as untrusted. Every byte Vault writes passes through the security barrier first, which encrypts it with 256-bit AES in Galois/Counter Mode and a fresh random nonce for each object. On a read, the authentication tag is verified, so if someone edits the stored bytes the check fails and Vault aborts the operation: tampering is detected, not only hidden. This covers all data Vault stores, such as policies, mount configuration and tokens, not just secret values. TLS to the storage backend is an optional extra layer, not a replacement for the barrier. Example: an attacker who copies the whole data directory of a stopped Vault node, but has no unseal shares and no token, sees only ciphertext and can learn little beyond the fact that secrets exist. The threat model does not promise protection against someone who can read the memory of a running, unsealed Vault or who controls the backend enough to delete or corrupt it.

concepts.heading: The Key Chain: Encryption Key, Root Key and Unseal Key
concepts.body: Three layers of keys sit between an operator and a stored secret. The encryption key lives in the keyring and encrypts almost everything Vault stores. The root key encrypts the encryption key, and the encrypted encryption key is stored next to the data. The unseal key encrypts the root key; with the default Shamir seal it is split into shares so no single person holds it. Unsealing walks back up the chain: shares rebuild the unseal key, the unseal key decrypts the root key, and the root key decrypts the encryption key. Layers keep maintenance cheap, because `vault operator rekey` changes the outer layer and only the small root key is re-encrypted, never the stored data. Do not confuse these with the initial root token: that is a client token with the `root` policy used to call the API and has nothing to do with the key chain. Data encryption key rotation (`vault operator rotate`) adds a new key term to the keyring.

concepts.heading: Initialization: vault operator init
concepts.body: A brand-new Vault has an empty storage backend and no keys at all, so `vault status` shows `Initialized false` and `Sealed true`. `vault operator init` prepares the storage: it generates the root key, stores it encrypted, splits the unseal key into shares and prints them with an initial root token. It happens once per cluster, not per node: HA nodes sharing one storage backend are initialized together, and running init again is refused because new keys would orphan the old data. Defaults are `-key-shares=5` and `-key-threshold=3`, with the threshold at most the share count. With auto-unseal, `-recovery-shares` and `-recovery-threshold` apply instead. To keep plaintext away from the terminal, `-pgp-keys` encrypts each share for one holder and `-root-token-pgp-key` encrypts the root token. A script can ask `vault operator init -status`, whose exit code is 0 when initialized, 1 on error and 2 when not initialized. With a Shamir seal the server is still sealed after init, and it holds no mounts or policies yet.

concepts.heading: Seal and Unseal in Practice
concepts.body: A sealed Vault can reach storage but cannot decrypt it, so the only things it can do are report status and accept unseal shares. A node becomes sealed again when `vault operator seal` is called, when the process restarts (a node with auto-unseal then unseals itself), or when storage hits an unrecoverable error; token revocation or lease expiry never seals it. With a Shamir seal, each `vault operator unseal` adds one share, in any order and from different machines, because progress is kept on the server and shown as `Unseal Progress` in `vault status`. Run it without an argument so the share is prompted and hidden instead of landing in shell history, and use `-reset` to discard partial progress. Sealing is the emergency brake: one operator is enough, but `sys/seal` is root-protected, so a policy needs `update` plus `sudo` on it. `vault status` exit codes describe seal state: 0 unsealed, 1 error, 2 sealed. Load balancers use the status endpoint for health checks because it answers even when sealed.

concepts.heading: CLI Environment Variables
concepts.body: The CLI reads its settings from environment variables, and a flag on one command overrides the variable for that command. `VAULT_ADDR` (flag `-address`) is where requests go; unset, it defaults to `https://127.0.0.1:8200`, which is why a laptop CLI that talks to a remote server needs it exported. `VAULT_TOKEN` supplies a token without `vault login`, which otherwise caches one through the token helper in `~/.vault-token`. `VAULT_CACERT` points to a PEM file of the CA to trust, and `VAULT_CAPATH` to a directory of them; both keep verification on, whereas `VAULT_SKIP_VERIFY` turns it off and is not appropriate for production. `VAULT_NAMESPACE` selects a namespace on Vault Enterprise or HCP Vault, and Community Vault has none. `VAULT_FORMAT` sets table, json, yaml or jsonx output, handy for a script that pipes `vault status` into `jq`, and it is separate from `VAULT_LOG_FORMAT`, which is for server logs. A token in the environment can leak, so prefer short-lived tokens.

examPoints: A question about what an attacker can read from copied storage files points to the barrier: everything is AES-GCM encrypted and the keys are protected by the root key, which is protected by the unseal key.

A question about unseal progress, shares entered from different workstations, or a wrong share points to the stateful unseal process: the server remembers shares until the threshold is met, the node is sealed, or `-reset` is used.
A question where the CLI hits 127.0.0.1 or fails TLS validation with a private CA points to `VAULT_ADDR` or `VAULT_CACERT`, never to skipping verification.

quiz.q: Three operators each hold one share of a five-share, threshold-three seal. Operator one enters a share from a laptop at 18:00 and leaves; the next morning operator two enters a different share from another laptop, then operator three enters a third from a third machine, all against the same node and with no restart or seal in between. What is the result?
choices: The node stays sealed, because every share must be entered from the same client session within a single command run
The node stays sealed, because shares entered on different days are discarded when the unseal command exits
The node unseals, because the server keeps accepted shares until the threshold is met, whichever client sent them
The node unseals after operator two, because any two shares are enough once a first share was recorded
quiz.explain: Unsealing is stateful: the server remembers accepted shares until the threshold is reached, the node is sealed, or `-reset` is run. Clients, machines and elapsed time do not matter. The threshold stays three, so two shares are not enough.

quiz.q: Two of five unseal key holders leave a company that uses a Shamir seal, and the security team runs `vault operator rekey` with the current threshold of shares and new settings. Which data does Vault re-encrypt as a result?
choices: Only the root key, now protected by a new unseal key; the stored data and the encryption key are left unchanged
Every secret and policy in storage, which is why a rekey of a large cluster is a long maintenance window
The encryption key and all stored data, while the root key is untouched and keeps its old unseal key
Only the initial root token, which is reissued so that the departed holders cannot use any older tokens
quiz.explain: Rekeying replaces the unseal key shares, so only the small root key is re-encrypted under the new unseal key. Stored data and the encryption key stay as they are, and tokens are not affected. Old shares stop being valid once the rekey completes.

days.recap: The barrier encrypts everything before it reaches untrusted storage; the unseal key protects the root key, which protects the encryption key, which protects the data. Init runs once, a restart seals a Shamir node, and the CLI is steered by VAULT_ADDR, VAULT_TOKEN and VAULT_CACERT.

days.title: Vault Cluster Strategy: Integrated Storage, Consul, HA and the Active Node

concepts.heading: Cluster Strategy: Why Run More Than One Node
concepts.body: A single Vault server is a single point of failure and every restart seals it, so production designs run a cluster of server nodes. Two ideas must stay separate. High availability (HA) protects against an outage: one node is active and the others wait to take over. Scaling work is a different goal, and standard HA does not provide it because only the active node processes requests; Vault is bound by storage I/O. A third idea is replication between whole clusters, which is Vault Enterprise only and appears on day 13. Choosing a strategy starts from requirements: how many simultaneous failures must be survived, where the data is stored, and who operates the storage. Example: a company that needs to survive the loss of two machines at once plans five nodes with Integrated Storage in one region, then adds Vault Enterprise replication only if it must also survive the loss of the whole region or serve distant users.

concepts.heading: Integrated Storage and Quorum
concepts.body: Integrated Storage is storage built into Vault and based on the Raft consensus protocol. HashiCorp recommends it for most use cases: it needs no extra software, adds no network hop, keeps encrypted data on the Vault hosts themselves, and leaves Vault as the only system to monitor. Before Vault 1.4 Consul was the recommended storage. Raft commits a change only when a majority of voters has stored it, and quorum is that majority. Three servers have quorum 2 and tolerate 1 failure, five have quorum 3 and tolerate 2, seven have quorum 4 and tolerate 3. Failure tolerance is cluster size minus quorum, so a fourth node adds no tolerance over three and an even size can stall a vote; use odd sizes. A two-node cluster has quorum 2, so one failure blocks writes and recovery is manual. If quorum is lost the cluster cannot elect a leader or commit writes. Example: five nodes lose two in a power cut and keep running, because three is still a majority.

concepts.heading: Joining Nodes and Autopilot
concepts.body: Only the first node of a cluster is initialized. Every other node starts with a `storage "raft"` block that has its own `node_id`, then joins with `vault operator raft join https://vault-1.example.com:8200`, or joins by itself at startup when the block carries a `retry_join` stanza. A joining node learns the peer set from the cluster, so it never runs `vault operator init`. With a Shamir seal it must still be unsealed, while with auto-unseal it unseals itself. Autopilot is on by default for Integrated Storage and decides whether a node is healthy enough to vote. A new node enters as a non-voter, syncs to the current Raft index, and becomes a voter only after the stability threshold passes. Dead server cleanup, enabled through the Autopilot API, removes unhealthy nodes automatically. Without this safeguard a syncing node would count toward quorum without being able to vote, so adding several at once could lose quorum.

concepts.heading: Consul and Other External Storage
concepts.body: Vault also runs on external backends such as Consul, with limited HashiCorp support and more operational work, because the external system must itself be clustered for HA. Compared with Integrated Storage, Consul needs a Vault cluster plus a dedicated Consul cluster, keeps its data in memory so snapshots matter more, and has a smaller default maximum entry size (512 KiB for Consul against 1 MiB for Integrated Storage, both configurable). A Consul cluster used for Vault storage should be dedicated, not shared with service discovery or service mesh. The example to remember is a team with existing Consul that must run Vault: that is a legitimate choice, but a new design without Consul takes Integrated Storage. Some backends hold both data and the HA lock, and a split mode is possible: `storage` names the backend that holds data and `ha_storage` names a different backend that manages the lock. For instance, `storage "s3"` for data with `ha_storage "consul"` for the lock. Unseal keys are never stored there in plaintext.

concepts.heading: HA, the Active Node and Standbys
concepts.body: When the storage backend supports HA, Vault enters HA mode automatically. One node takes a lock and becomes active; the rest are standbys. A standby that receives a request forwards it to the active node, since request forwarding is on by default, or answers with a `307` redirect to the configured `api_addr`. If the active node is sealed, fails or loses connectivity, an unsealed standby takes the lock. This is why standbys must be unsealed: a sealed node cannot take part, and a node sealed with `vault operator seal` stays sealed until it is restarted or unsealed through the unseal API. Monitor seal status on every node and keep a standby after patching. Standard standbys only forward, so HA adds availability and no throughput. In Vault Enterprise, performance standbys serve read-only requests, such as KV reads and transit calls, and forward anything that writes storage; they live inside one cluster and share its storage, unlike replication, which links separate clusters.

examPoints: A question about a node count, a failure scenario or adding a fourth or sixth node is testing quorum: tolerance equals nodes minus quorum, and odd sizes are recommended.
A question that asks for the recommended storage for a new self-managed cluster points to Integrated Storage; Consul or other external backends are possible but need extra infrastructure.
A question about adding throughput with standby nodes is a trap: standard HA gives availability only, and only Vault Enterprise performance standbys serve reads.

quiz.q: A team runs a seven-node Integrated Storage cluster. Three nodes lose power at once for twenty minutes. What is the state of the cluster during the outage?
choices: It cannot elect a leader, because losing more than two nodes breaks the majority needed for any commit
It keeps its leader and accepts writes, because four of seven voters remain and quorum is four
It accepts reads only, because writes require every node that was part of the peer set at startup
It runs unchanged, because standby nodes are not counted in the Raft peer set for quorum
quiz.explain: Quorum for seven voters is four, so the four surviving nodes still form a majority and the cluster keeps working; failure tolerance is seven minus four, which is three. Only a fourth failure would stop commits and leader elections.

quiz.q: A load balancer sends a client write to a standby node in a standard HA cluster with default settings. The client then complains that the cluster 'does not scale' even after nodes were added. Which statement is accurate?
choices: The standby rejects the write with an error, because only the active node may receive client requests
The standby seals itself, because accepting a client request would break its standby role
The standby handles the write locally and syncs it later, so adding nodes should raise throughput
The standby forwards the request to the active node, so more standbys add availability but not throughput
quiz.explain: With request forwarding on by default, a standby passes requests to the active node (or redirects with a 307 to `api_addr`). Only the active node processes requests in standard HA, so extra nodes improve availability, not throughput. Read scaling needs Vault Enterprise performance standbys.

days.recap: Run odd-sized clusters of Raft Integrated Storage, the recommended backend, where tolerance is nodes minus quorum. One node is active and unsealed standbys take over, but standard HA adds availability, not throughput; Consul and ha_storage are the external option.

days.title: Shamir Shares, Auto-Unseal, Replication in Vault Enterprise, and Self-Managed versus HCP Vault Dedicated

concepts.heading: Shamir's Secret Sharing
concepts.body: By default Vault splits the unseal key with Shamir's Secret Sharing. `-key-shares` sets how many shares exist and `-key-threshold` how many are needed to rebuild the key; the defaults are 5 and 3 and the threshold cannot exceed the shares. Any threshold-sized subset works in any order, and fewer shares reveal nothing about the key. Holders can enter shares from different machines. Losing shares is tolerable up to shares minus threshold, so with 7 shares and a threshold of 3 up to four holders can vanish, but one more loss makes unsealing impossible. When holders leave, run `vault operator rekey` while the threshold is still met: it asks for the current shares, lets you pick new `-key-shares` and `-key-threshold` (and PGP keys), and afterwards the old shares are no longer valid. The weakness of the Shamir seal is automation: every restarted node is sealed again and needs people, which is awkward for nodes that are replaced often.

concepts.heading: Auto-Unseal and Recovery Keys
concepts.body: Auto-unseal hands protection of the unseal key to a trusted external service, such as a cloud KMS, an HSM or another Vault's transit engine. At startup Vault asks that service to decrypt the root key, so nobody types shares and nodes in autoscaling groups come up unsealed. The key chain still exists; only the outer step changes. Initialization then returns recovery keys instead of unseal keys, controlled by `-recovery-shares` and `-recovery-threshold` (defaults 5 and 3). Recovery keys cannot decrypt the root key and cannot unseal; they authorize operations that need a quorum of humans, such as `vault operator generate-root` and `vault operator rekey`. To change the recovery shares use `vault operator rekey -target=recovery`. The price is a lifecycle dependency: if the KMS key is disabled or permanently deleted before a seal migration, the cluster cannot be unsealed, even from backups. Vault Enterprise Seal HA allows two or three auto seals so one unreachable seal does not block startup.

concepts.heading: Seal Migration
concepts.body: Switching seal type is rare, so HashiCorp accepts brief downtime for it. Moving from Shamir to auto-unseal means taking a backup, adding the new seal block to the configuration while the old seal is still available, restarting, and running `vault operator unseal -migrate` with the Shamir keys. Those Shamir keys then become the recovery keys of the auto seal. With Integrated Storage a quorum of nodes must be back for the leader to perform the migration. Online migration with Seal HA is a Vault Enterprise option for auto seals and does not support Shamir. Example: a team that outgrows manual unsealing plans a short window, migrates three nodes to a KMS seal, then protects the KMS key with strict permissions so nobody schedules it for deletion. Do not confuse `-migrate` with `-reset`, which only discards partial unseal progress.

concepts.heading: Replication: DR versus Performance (Vault Enterprise)
concepts.body: Replication links separate clusters and is Vault Enterprise only. Disaster recovery (DR) replication builds a warm standby that mirrors the primary, including tokens, leases and local mounts; it serves no client requests until promoted, and after promotion clients can keep their existing tokens and leases. Performance replication creates secondaries that serve clients locally, which cuts latency and scales reads: shared configuration, policies and secrets such as KV values and transit keys replicate, while each secondary keeps its own tokens and leases, so clients re-authenticate after a promotion. A write to replicated data is forwarded to the primary, and during a lost link a performance secondary still serves reads (possibly stale) but cannot write replicated data. Mounts created with `-local` do not reach performance secondaries but do reach DR secondaries. A paths filter can deny selected mounts or namespaces per secondary for data residency. Activating a secondary replaces its seal keys or recovery keys with the primary's.

concepts.heading: Self-Managed versus HCP Vault Dedicated
concepts.body: HCP Vault Dedicated is a hosted Vault Enterprise run by HashiCorp, with the same binary, CLI, API and UI. The difference is who does the platform work. On a self-managed cluster you choose the storage backend and seal, install and upgrade Vault, take backups and snapshots, and keep the cluster healthy. On HCP Vault Dedicated the cluster uses Integrated Storage and auto-unseal with a unique KMS key, and HashiCorp handles upgrades, backups, snapshots, cluster health and HA operations. HSM auto-unseal is not offered there. Customers still configure authentication methods, policies, secrets engines and identity, and they manage tokens, leases and old secret versions. Initialization also differs: a self-managed init prints unseal or recovery keys and a `root` token, and the top-level namespace is `root`, whereas on HCP administrators generate an `admin` token in the HCP Portal and the top-level namespace is `admin`. Teams therefore set up auth methods and policies early so daily work does not depend on that token.

examPoints: A question about who may generate a root token or rekey on an auto-unseal cluster is testing recovery keys, which authorize operations but can never unseal or decrypt the root key.

A question where applications must keep existing tokens and leases after a regional failover points to DR replication; a question about low-latency reads in another region points to performance replication, and both are Vault Enterprise.
A question about what HashiCorp does on HCP Vault Dedicated covers upgrades, backups and HA operations, but not your policies, auth methods, secrets engines or tokens.

quiz.q: An operator needs a new root token on a cluster that unseals itself through a cloud KMS. The cluster started normally this morning. Which credentials authorize `vault operator generate-root`?
choices: A threshold of unseal key shares, which are printed by init for every cluster regardless of the seal type configured
The KMS key identifier, which Vault checks against the configured seal before it issues any new root token at all
A threshold of recovery keys, because auto-unseal clusters use them for operations that need a quorum of operators
The previous root token, because an expired or revoked root token can be replaced by presenting it one more time
quiz.explain: With auto-unseal, init returns recovery keys, and they authorize quorum operations such as `generate-root` and `rekey`. They cannot unseal. A Shamir cluster would ask for unseal key shares, and the KMS identifier is not a credential for this operation.

quiz.q: A security engineer is told that a Vault Enterprise cluster will move from a self-managed deployment to HCP Vault Dedicated. Which task remains the customer's responsibility after the move?
choices: Defining policies and enabling auth methods and secrets engines for each application team
Taking snapshots and backups of the cluster before every upgrade window and storing them safely
Choosing and operating the storage backend and its HA configuration for each of the nodes
Performing minor and major version upgrades and checking the health of the whole cluster
quiz.explain: HashiCorp operates the platform on HCP Vault Dedicated: Integrated Storage, auto-unseal, upgrades, backups and HA operations. Configuration of auth methods, policies, secrets engines and identity, and handling of tokens and leases, stays with the customer.

days.recap: Shamir splits the unseal key and tolerates losing shares minus threshold of them; auto-unseal uses a KMS, HSM or transit and gives recovery keys that authorize but never unseal. DR keeps tokens and leases and serves nothing until promoted, performance serves clients locally; HCP Vault Dedicated runs the platform.

days.title: Vault Agent and Vault Secrets Operator: Delivering Secrets to Applications

concepts.heading: Why a Client Daemon: Vault Agent
concepts.body: Many applications cannot or should not contain Vault client code, for example a legacy program that reads a password from a properties file. Vault Agent is a client daemon that runs next to the application and talks to Vault for it. Its main features are auto-auth, which logs in using a chosen method and keeps the token renewed; sinks, which write that token to a file; templating, which renders secrets into files using Consul Template markup; caching of tokens and leased secrets; and process supervisor mode, which injects secrets as environment variables. Agent is an ordinary daemon, so it runs under systemd on a virtual machine as well as in Kubernetes as a sidecar or init container. Example: a template such as `{{ with secret "secret/db" }}{{ .Data.data.password }}{{ end }}` writes the password into the file the application already opens, and Agent renders it again when the secret changes.

concepts.heading: Auto-Auth and Sinks
concepts.body: Auto-auth removes the login step from the application. Agent authenticates with a method suited to where it runs (AppRole, Kubernetes, AWS and others), keeps the token renewed, and re-authenticates when it expires. The `kubernetes` method reads the pod's service account token from the default path and sends it with the configured `role` to the auth method at `auth/kubernetes`, so no secret has to be copied into the pod. Failed logins retry with exponential backoff: `min_backoff` (default 1s) doubles each time and `max_backoff` (default 5m) caps the delay between attempts, not the total time. `exit_on_err` makes Agent exit on login errors, and `exit_after_auth` makes it exit with code 0 after one successful authentication, useful for init containers and one-off jobs. A sink writes the token to a file, and the token can be response-wrapped in the method block (the client can verify where it came from but must renew it) or in the sink block (Agent keeps renewing). Auto-auth does not support tokens with a limited number of uses, so use `token_num_uses=0` on the role.

concepts.heading: Templates, Caching and Process Supervisor Mode
concepts.body: Templates refresh at different moments depending on the secret. Renewable secrets and tokens renew after two thirds of the lease has passed. Non-leased secrets such as KV v2 are fetched every 5 minutes by default, changed with `static_secret_render_interval` in `template_config`. Non-renewable leased secrets, such as many database credentials, are fetched again near 90 percent of the TTL. If a secret exists but a key is missing, the engine prints `<no value>` unless `error_on_missing_key = true` is set. Caching holds tokens and leased secrets and renews them; it does not cache static KV secrets. Entries are evicted when they cannot be renewed or when a revoke passes through Agent, but a revocation done straight against Vault is invisible to it. In process supervisor mode Agent renders each `env_template` and starts one child from a top-level `exec` block; because environment variables cannot change in a running process, `restart_on_secret_changes` defaults to `always` and restarts the child when a secret changes.

concepts.heading: Vault Secrets Operator
concepts.body: The Vault Secrets Operator (VSO) is a Kubernetes operator that syncs Vault secrets into native Kubernetes Secrets, declared as custom resources, with no sidecar in the pods and no application changes. Two foundation resources describe access. `VaultConnection` holds the Vault address and TLS settings, and `VaultAuth` holds the login method (kubernetes, jwt, appRole, aws or gcp), mount and role, and refers to a connection. A VaultAuth can be used by secret resources in its own namespace unless `allowedNamespaces` lists others or `["*"]`. Each secret class has its own resource: `VaultStaticSecret` for KV v1 and v2, `VaultDynamicSecret` for engines that issue credentials such as database or AWS (with `allowStaticCreds: true` for rotated static roles), and `VaultPKISecret` for certificates. A `destination` names the Kubernetes Secret, and `transformation` can exclude or include fields. KV has no lease, so `refreshAfter` sets how often to sync, and `rolloutRestartTargets` restart Deployments, DaemonSets or StatefulSets when a secret changes, which matters for environment variables.

concepts.heading: Which Delivery Model to Choose
concepts.body: Choose by who must be Vault-aware and where the workload runs. Direct API or a client library gives the most control, for example calling `transit/encrypt` with application data on each request, but the application must know Vault. Agent needs no application change and works anywhere, including virtual machines, at the cost of one Agent per workload or host. The Vault Agent Injector automates the Agent sidecar and init container in Kubernetes with annotations and renders secrets to a memory volume in the pod, not into Kubernetes Secrets. VSO suits a platform team with hundreds of workloads that want secrets as Kubernetes Secrets, one operator per cluster, and normal Kubernetes access control (RBAC). Because VSO creates Kubernetes Secrets, protect them with RBAC and encryption at rest. VSO and the Injector are Kubernetes-only; Agent is not. Example: applications on virtual machines that read a config file and rotate secrets every few hours need Agent templates, while a service that encrypts each record calls transit directly.

examPoints: A question where an application on a virtual machine cannot be changed and reads a file points to Vault Agent templates; VSO and the Injector work only in Kubernetes.
A question about native Kubernetes Secrets with no sidecar per pod points to the Vault Secrets Operator, and the secret type (KV, dynamic credentials, certificate) picks the resource kind.
A question about per-request operations such as transit encrypt of application data points to direct API calls, since Agent templates and VSO fetch secrets from fixed paths ahead of time.

quiz.q: An operator edits a KV v2 secret in Vault. An application on a virtual machine reads that secret through a file rendered by a Vault Agent template, and the file takes several minutes to change. The team wants updates to arrive within about a minute. Which change fits?
choices: Set `static_secret_render_interval` in `template_config` to a shorter value, because KV v2 has no lease and is polled
Set `lease_renewal_threshold` lower, because the file refreshes only at a set fraction of the KV lease duration
Enable `exit_after_auth`, so that Agent logs in again and renders the template after each secret change
Turn on persistent caching, because cached KV entries must be evicted before the template can be rendered
quiz.explain: KV v2 secrets are non-leased, so Agent fetches them on a timer, every 5 minutes by default, and `static_secret_render_interval` changes it. Lease-based settings do not apply to KV, `exit_after_auth` stops the Agent, and static KV secrets are not cached.

quiz.q: A platform team needs a Kubernetes Secret that holds AWS credentials issued on request from the AWS secrets engine at aws/creds/deploy, renewed by the system before they expire. Which Vault Secrets Operator resource is appropriate?
choices: `VaultStaticSecret`, because the source path names one fixed secret that the operator reads on a timer
`VaultPKISecret`, because every short-lived credential is treated as a certificate request
`VaultConnection`, because it holds the address and the path of the credentials to sync
`VaultDynamicSecret`, because it syncs engines that issue leased credentials and renews the lease
quiz.explain: Engines that issue credentials, such as AWS and database, are synced with `VaultDynamicSecret`, which renews the lease or requests new credentials when it expires. `VaultStaticSecret` is for KV, `VaultPKISecret` for certificates, and `VaultConnection` only describes the Vault server.

days.recap: Agent is a client daemon with auto-auth, sinks, templates, caching and supervisor mode, works on virtual machines or Kubernetes, and polls non-leased KV on an interval. VSO syncs Vault secrets into Kubernetes Secrets through CRDs (static, dynamic, PKI); direct API calls stay right for per-request work like transit.

days.title: Final Review: Exam Format, the Nine Objectives, Commonly Confused Pairs and Test-Day Plan

concepts.heading: Know the Exam Format
concepts.body: The HashiCorp Certified: Vault Associate (003) exam lasts 1 hour, is proctored online, is given in English, costs USD 70.50 and the certification is valid for 2 years. It tests Vault 1.19. Question types are true or false, multiple choice and multiple answer, the same as the Terraform Associate, and a multiple answer question says how many options to pick, so choose exactly that many. The number of questions, the pass mark and the weight of each objective are not published, so do not rely on a rumored number and spread your preparation evenly. The audience is a cloud engineer with foundational Vault knowledge, and the questions test decisions and predictions, such as which token type, which policy or what happens on revoke, more than trivia. With one hour and an unpublished question count, answer what you know first, flag the rest, and keep a steady pace.

concepts.heading: The Nine Objectives in One Pass
concepts.body: Use this list as a final checklist; headings are the official objective names. 1 Authentication methods: purpose, choosing by use case, human versus machine methods (humans with userpass, LDAP or OIDC; machines with AppRole, Kubernetes, cloud or TLS certificates), identities and groups, and using or configuring them by CLI, API or UI. 2 Vault policies: deny by default, path syntax with exact, `+` and `*`, capabilities including `sudo` and `deny`, choosing by requirements, KV v2 `data` and `metadata` paths. 3 Vault tokens: service versus batch, root tokens, accessors, TTL and max TTL, orphan and periodic tokens, `vault token create`. 4 Vault leases: lease IDs, renew, revoke by ID or prefix. 5 Secrets engines: choosing KV, database, AWS, PKI, transit or cubbyhole, static versus dynamic secrets, response wrapping, enabling and reading by CLI, API and UI. 6 Encryption as a Service: transit encrypt, decrypt, key rotation. 7 Vault architecture fundamentals: how Vault encrypts data, seal and unseal, environment variables. 8 Vault deployment architecture: cluster strategy, storage backends, Shamir, replication, self-managed versus HCP Vault Dedicated. 9 Access management architecture: Vault Agent and the Vault Secrets Operator.

concepts.heading: Confused Pairs: Auth, Policies, Tokens and Leases
concepts.body: An entity is the identity of a person or machine, and an alias links it to a login on one auth method; internal groups are managed in Vault, external groups map to groups in an outside provider. Humans usually log in with userpass, LDAP or OIDC, while machines use AppRole, Kubernetes or cloud identity. In policies, `+` matches exactly one path segment and `*` is a glob only at the end; `deny` always wins, and a deny-by-default posture means no policy means no access. With KV v2 the API path has `data/` or `metadata/` in it, so `vault kv get secret/app` needs `read` on `secret/data/app`, whereas `vault read secret/app` would not add that prefix. Service tokens are renewable and can have children; batch tokens are lightweight, not renewable and cannot create children. A token accessor can look up or revoke a token but is not the token. TTL is renewable up to max TTL, a periodic token has no max TTL and lives while renewed, and an orphan token survives revocation of its parent. Revoking a token revokes its child tokens and leases, `vault lease revoke -prefix` revokes a whole path, and a renewed lease cannot exceed its max TTL.

concepts.heading: Confused Pairs: Engines, Transit, Architecture and Delivery
concepts.body: KV holds static secrets you store; database, AWS and similar engines issue dynamic ones with leases, which limits exposure. Cubbyhole is private to one token, and response wrapping returns a single-use wrapping token whose content sits in a cubbyhole until unwrapped. Transit encrypts data you send and stores none of it: plaintext is base64, ciphertext looks like `vault:v1:...`, `rotate` adds a key version, `min_decryption_version` blocks older versions, and `rewrap` moves ciphertext to the latest version without exposing plaintext. The root key is part of the barrier chain, the root token is a client token. Unseal keys unseal, recovery keys only authorize quorum operations on an auto-unseal cluster. `init` runs once per cluster, `unseal` runs per node, and `seal` needs sudo. Integrated Storage is recommended over Consul, and HA adds availability, not throughput. Vault Enterprise DR replication keeps tokens and leases and serves nothing until promoted, performance replication serves clients and keeps its own tokens and leases. HCP Vault Dedicated runs the platform, you run the policies. Agent works anywhere and is configured per host; the Secrets Operator syncs into Kubernetes Secrets in a cluster.

concepts.heading: Test-Day Plan
concepts.body: Before the exam, sleep, check your identification and prepare the proctored environment: a clear desk, a working camera and microphone, a stable connection, and the provider's system check run beforehand. Make a first pass: answer what you know at once, mark uncertain items and keep moving. On each question read the last line first to see what is asked, then look for deciding clues in the stem: a command name, a token type, a path with or without `data/`, whether the node is sealed, whether it is Vault Enterprise or HCP. On multiple answer items find the count and eliminate options that are too broad or that confuse a pair above. Watch for absolute words like always and never. When two options both seem right, pick the one the documentation recommends, such as Integrated Storage, short-lived dynamic secrets and least-privilege policies. Spend leftover time on flagged items, and change an answer only if you can name the clue that makes the new one better. Afterwards, note weak topics and use the question bank to drill them.

examPoints: The exam is 1 hour, online proctored, tests Vault 1.19, and mixes true or false, multiple choice and multiple answer items; the question count and pass mark are not published, so prepare evenly across all nine objectives.

The commonly confused pairs (service and batch tokens, TTL and max TTL, root key and root token, unseal and recovery keys, DR and performance replication, Agent and VSO) are favorite wrong answers: name what each one does before you choose.
On the day, read what is asked, find the clue (command, path, token type, seal state, edition), eliminate by the confusion pairs, and flag rather than stall.

quiz.q: A token has this policy: `path "secret/app" { capabilities = ["read"] }`. The `secret/` mount is KV v2, and `vault kv get secret/app` returns a permission denied error. What is the correct fix?
choices: Change the capability to `list`, because reading a KV v2 secret needs list on the same path
Change the path to `secret/data/app`, because the KV v2 API path for secret data includes `data/`
Add `sudo` to the capabilities, because KV v2 secrets are root-protected paths
Change the path to `secret/metadata/app`, because `vault kv get` reads the metadata of the secret first
quiz.explain: On KV v2, `vault kv get secret/app` calls the API path `secret/data/app`, so the policy must grant `read` there. `metadata/` is for version and deletion metadata and for listing, and `sudo` is not needed for KV reads.

quiz.q: An application stored customer records with transit key `orders`, and ciphertexts start with `vault:v1:`. The key was rotated twice since, and the team wants all stored ciphertext moved to the latest version without any service seeing plaintext. Which approach does this?
choices: Decrypt each value with `transit/decrypt/orders`, then encrypt it again with the application's own library
Raise `min_decryption_version` for the key, because Vault re-encrypts old ciphertext when old versions are blocked
Call `transit/rewrap/orders` for each ciphertext, which returns it under the latest key version inside Vault
Rotate the key once more, because each rotation re-encrypts every ciphertext already issued by that key
quiz.explain: Rewrap decrypts and re-encrypts inside Vault, so plaintext never leaves it and the result is `vault:v3:` or newer. Rotation only adds a version for new encryptions, and raising `min_decryption_version` would make old ciphertext undecryptable rather than upgrade it.

days.recap: Walk the nine objectives once, then drill the confused pairs: tokens, leases, KV v2 paths, transit versions, unseal versus recovery keys, DR versus performance, Agent versus VSO. Expect 1 hour, Vault 1.19, no published pass mark; read the ask, find the clue, flag and move on.
